topStories.headline: Bare Bones Opens on Taraval, Nippon Curry Heads to Irving as Sunset's Restaurant Scene Keeps Rolling
topStories.dek: A rotisserie chicken counter is now open in Parkside and a Japanese curry chain has signed on for Irving Street, adding momentum to both of the Sunset's main commercial corridors.
topStories.body:
A rotisserie chicken restaurant called Bare Bones opened last week at 2325 Taraval St. in the Parkside neighborhood, filling the space formerly occupied by the seafood spot Bearing West. The counter-service restaurant is run by three food-industry veterans who met at their children's preschool and builds its menu around slow-cooked birds. Hand-painted purple-and-pink signs by artist Jeff Canham mark the storefront, which the SF Standard had listed among the city's most-anticipated restaurant openings for November.

Across the district on Irving Street, Nippon Curry — a Bay Area Japanese curry chain with existing locations in the Marina, Berkeley, and San Jose — has taken over the former Lomo Libre space at Irving and 19th Avenue. The restaurant serves pork katsu and karaage curry and is planning a second Sunset location as part of a broader San Francisco expansion.

The new arrivals land at a moment when the two corridors are tracking differently. Inner Sunset sales tax revenue has recovered past its pre-pandemic peak, driven by a wave of restaurant openings near Ninth and Irving, where a new Neapolitan pizzeria from world-renowned chef Vincenzo Capuano is also in the works at 822 Irving St. Meanwhile, Taraval and Noriega streets have been slower to rebound, with Parkside merchants pointing partly to parking losses from the ongoing L-Taraval rail project. Albert Chow, president of People of Parkside Sunset, has said the loss of parking spots has deterred drivers from frequenting Taraval businesses. Bare Bones' arrival is being watched by local merchants as a potential sign of recovery on that corridor.

topStories.headline: Outer Sunset Soup Counter Rusty Ladle Takes San Francisco's Best Chowder Crown
topStories.dek: Chef-owner John Lindsey beat out Fisherman's Wharf and North Beach institutions at Chowderfest 2026, putting his Lawton Street counter firmly on the city's culinary map.
topStories.body:
Rusty Ladle, a small soup counter at 3645 Lawton St. near 43rd Avenue in the Outer Sunset, won the top prize at this year's Fisherman's Wharf Chowderfest, taking the title of San Francisco's best clam chowder away from longtime favorites including Sotto Mare and Boudin. Chef-owner John Lindsey, a veteran of Hayes Street Grill, makes a gluten-free Bodega Bay-style chowder thickened with potato starch. The win was reported in Mission Local's Sunset Buzz column on November 6.

Rusty Ladle operates out of a narrow 700-square-foot storefront and also serves a rotating lineup of seasonal soups alongside a signature inside-out grilled cheese called the Schmelty. The restaurant shares a parklet with Andytown Coffee Roasters next door and is open Thursday through Sunday.

The recognition brings fresh citywide attention to a part of the Outer Sunset that has long played second fiddle to the busier Inner Sunset strip. Lindsey has said he aims to open two additional San Francisco locations.

topStories.headline: Westside Voters Who Once Opposed Sunset Dunes Now Say They Can't Imagine Losing It
topStories.dek: Post-election analysis finds that Sunset and Richmond residents who voted against the original park measure two years ago flipped decisively to defeat Prop G on November 3.
topStories.body:
When San Francisco voters rejected Proposition G on November 3 — keeping cars off the former Great Highway and preserving Sunset Dunes park by a 63-to-37 margin — the most striking finding was where the opposition to reopening came from. Residents of the Sunset and Richmond districts, who had voted overwhelmingly against creating the park just two years earlier, reversed course and voted to protect it, according to post-election reporting by Mission Local published November 9.

The shift reflects how residents who live closest to the park have changed their relationship with it since it opened in March 2025. Many now use the two-mile car-free stretch along Ocean Beach to walk dogs, run, and teach children to ride bikes. What was once an abstract debate about traffic diversion became, for many westside residents, a question of whether to give up something they had come to depend on week after week.

Prop G was the third ballot measure in four years to put the future of the former roadway to a citywide vote. With its defeat, Sunset Dunes — which includes a skate park that opened in 2025 and a pirate-themed playground called Shipwreck Cove that opened in September 2026 — appears settled as a permanent park under the management of the San Francisco Recreation and Parks Department. The park has become the third most popular in San Francisco on weekdays, behind JFK Promenade and Marina Green.

moreNews.headline: Supervisor Alan Wong Re-Elected to Full Term Representing the Sunset
moreNews.body: District 4 Supervisor Alan Wong, whose district covers the Central and Outer Sunset, won a full four-year term at the November 3 election. Wong had first taken the seat after winning a special election in June 2026 to fill the remainder of Joel Engardio's term. He had been a prominent advocate for reopening the Great Highway to weekday traffic, a position rejected by voters citywide when Prop G went down to defeat on the same ballot.

moreNews.headline: Nutcracker Dancers to Bring Free Story Time to Sunset Branch Library This Holiday Season
moreNews.body: Dancers from Mark Foehringer's Nutcracker Sweets production will visit the Sunset Branch Library for a free story-time event aimed at children aged 5 and younger, in advance of the company's December 5–20 run at Cowell Theater at Fort Mason Center. The Richmond Sunset News reported the event in its November 11 announcements; specific dates for the Sunset Branch visit had not been confirmed at press time, so readers should check directly with the branch for scheduling.
